title: Hospitality and service at Advanced
lead: The Court's 2025 Advanced and Master service standards: hospitality, price and problems, the general routine, sparkling and decanting, beer, sake, aperitifs, digestifs and cocktails, pairing and selling, and how the practical exam runs.

intro.title: THE 2025 STANDARDS
intro.text: The Court's Advanced and Master standards are the only service standards accepted at its exams. They are more formal than most restaurants on purpose.

lines.label: Presence
lines.text: Greet warmly and match your language to each guest's comfort and knowledge. Technical terms can confuse guests or push them away.

lines.label: Price
lines.text: Recommend inside the guest's budget. A pricier suggestion needs a clear explanation of the added value, so the guest trusts it.

know: Missing a guest's tastes risks discounts, comps, bad reviews and lost loyalty.
Watch verbal and nonverbal cues: tone, wording and body language, from arrival to departure.
Problem resolution in three steps: acknowledge, apologize sincerely, act quickly and kindly.
Find the host's budget discreetly; if there isn't one, offer several price points.
Expect confrontational guests at Advanced, played by Master Sommeliers from a script.

sections.name: General service standards
sections.source: Court of Master Sommeliers, Americas, Advanced and Master Hospitality & Service Standards (2025); Advanced Theory Exam guide

lines.label: Setup
lines.text: Lists clean and accurate, glasses polished with linen and steam, tools organized. Only glass, plates, serviettes, silverware and underliners touch the cloth.

lines.label: The order
lines.text: Identify the host, stand to the ordering guest's right, and repeat the order back: vintage, producer, cuvée, style or quality level, and who gets what.

know: Serve from the guest's right when you can, and always move clockwise.
Bottles, decanters, ice buckets and corks sit on an underliner, never straight on the cloth.
Foil: two clean cuts just below the second lip, then into your pocket.
The taste pour is 1-1.5 oz (30-45 ml), label facing the ordering guest.
A guest of honor is served first; the ordering guest is always served last.

items.name: Confirm
items.text: Repeat vintage, producer, cuvée, style; say who gets what

items.name: Glasses
items.text: On a tray, right hand, guest's right; host or host's left first, clockwise

items.name: Present
items.text: From the ordering guest's right, with the full details

items.name: Open
items.text: Two cuts, wipe, quiet pull, wipe, cork on an underliner

items.name: Pour
items.text: 1-1.5 oz taste; left of the ordering guest, clockwise, host last

visuals.title: the taste pour
visuals.text: 30-45 ml for the ordering guest's approval, for still wine, sparkling and wine from a decanter.

sections.name: Sparkling and decanting
sections.source: Court of Master Sommeliers, Americas, Advanced and Master Hospitality & Service Standards (2025); example Advanced Practical feedback report

lines.label: Sparkling
lines.text: Two serviettes, two underliners, the bucket on a stand to the host's right. Open in the air or in the bucket, cutting below the cage with the blade.

lines.label: Decanting
lines.text: Three reasons: aeration, sediment, or raising the temperature 1 to 3 degrees. Confirm with the guest first; they make the final call.

know: Loosen the cage but never remove it; cork and cage come out together.
Turn the bottle, not the cork, at 45 degrees if possible. The ideal sound is a soft hiss.
Fill each sparkling glass in no more than two pours.
Sediment decanting takes three serviettes and three underliners: cork, bottle, decanter.
Upright bottle: keep it upright, no cradle. Stored on its side: cradle it that way, label up or not.

items.label: SPARKLING
items.title: Two of everything
items.text:
Serviette 1: dry, present, open
Serviette 2: lip and drips
Underliners: bottle, cork

items.label: SEDIMENT DECANT
items.title: Three of everything
items.text:
Serviettes: cradle, bottle lip, pouring
Underliners: cork, bottle, decanter
Light: candle or flashlight

items.name: Sediment
items.text: Slow, one smooth motion; stop when sediment reaches the shoulder

items.name: Double
items.text: Decant, rinse the bottle with wine, pour it back

items.name: Splash
items.text: Young, closed reds only; pour hard, invert if needed

items.name: Large format
items.text: Check the decanter's size; use several if needed

lines.label: Beer and sake
lines.text: Beer: repeat brewery, style and brand, open at the side station, leave about 1 inch (2-3 cm) of foam. Modern sake service follows white wine standards.

lines.label: Spirits
lines.text: Aperitifs and digestifs come from a tray or gueridon. Cocktails are shaken, stirred or built, and never finished on 'dirty rocks'.

know: Glass by beer style: pilsner flute, weizen glass, goblet/snifter, tulip, American pint, or an AP wine glass.
Hazy beers with sediment: ask whether the guest wants the sediment in the glass.
Mori koboshi: the ochoko overflows into the masu about halfway. Nigori: invert and swirl to mix the kasu.
Small tulip or copita for fortified wines and eaux de vie; rocks glass on ice; snifter for neat oak-aged spirits.
Never shake carbonated ingredients; stir with the mixing glass about three-quarters full of ice.

items.label: SHAKEN
items.title: In the shaker
items.text:
Muddle first if the recipe says
Don't overfill with ice
No carbonated ingredients before shaking

items.label: STIRRED
items.title: In the mixing glass
items.text:
Measure with a jigger
Ice about three-quarters full
Stir to chill and dilute, then strain

lines.label: Guest first
lines.text: The best pairing matches what the guest likes. If they want red wine with shellfish, honor it.

lines.label: Explain it
lines.text: Say why it works in appetizing, guest-friendly words, covering structure (acidity, tannin, body) and how the aromas and flavors fit.

know: Exam tasks: propose a pairing, weigh its strengths and weaknesses, judge suitability, explain your reasoning.
Pair beer, sake, spirits and non-alcoholic drinks too, not just wine.
Know classic and modern pairings, cooking techniques, iconic dishes and the key flavors of world cuisines.
Name the wine fully: producer, vintage and full appellation.
Ask what a guest will want to know about a beverage, and be ready to answer.

lines.label: Order
lines.text: Business of the Sommelier comes first (a timed, written exam), then Hospitality & Service right after.

lines.label: Prep
lines.text: About 15-20 minutes to study the situation, guest notes, menus, wine list and beverage list. Take notes on your pad, never on the menus.

know: Two tables per panel, with a maître d' who can't answer content or service questions.
Treat it as a very busy but manageable evening: every movement must count.
Suspend disbelief: signs on the prep table show which beverages are being ordered.
Finish your first table early and you'll be asked to face a wall.
The Practical needs 60%; a first Practical below 40% means an extra year's wait.

mixups.why: Splash is fast and hard, for young closed reds. Sediment decanting is slow and smooth, for old or unfiltered wines.
The taste pour is 1-1.5 oz for approval. Priming uses 1-2 oz to coat the glass or decanter, only on request.
Mori koboshi is a pouring style that overflows into the masu. Nigori is a cloudy sake with kasu.
The maître d' directs you and can't answer content questions. The guests are Master Sommeliers playing roles.

facts.fact: 2025 standards cover general hospitality, general service, sparkling, decanting, other wine service, beer, sake, aperitif and digestif, cocktail service and food and beverage pairing. They are more formal and exacting than many restaurants on purpose.
The Hospitality & Service standards published by the CMS-A are the only accepted service standards for any CMS-A examination.

Hospitality is about making guests feel welcomed, valued and understood. Without attentiveness the experience risks guest dissatisfaction, revenue loss through discounts or comps, and long-term impact through negative reviews or lower loyalty.
Tableside presence: warm greeting; adjust language to each guest's comfort and knowledge; technical or overly complex terms can confuse or distance guests.
Price point: balance recommendations with salesmanship that fits the guest's budget; suggesting a more expensive option must come with a clear explanation showing added value and building trust.

Guest satisfaction: attend to verbal and nonverbal cues, check in when appropriate, listen to tone and wording, observe physical cues, stay present from arrival to departure. Problem resolution: acknowledge the issue (listen actively), apologize sincerely (focus on how it made the guest feel), act quickly and kindly.

Demeanor: discreetly determine if the host has a budget; if not, offer several selections at different price points; when in doubt, undersell. Problem resolution has six suggested steps, starting with recognizing the problem and engaging the guest.
Advanced Sommeliers must handle uncomfortable situations at the table, which may include Master Sommeliers portraying confrontational guests while playing a role and reading from a script.

Mise en place: beverage lists clean, accurate, up to date, easy to read; glasses spotless, odor-free, polished with clean linen and steam; serviettes folded; underliners clean; only glassware, plates, serviettes, silverware and underliners placed directly on the tablecloth; bottles, decanters, ice buckets and corks on an underliner; a tray that isn't non-slip is lined with a serviette.
General guidelines: serve from the guest's right whenever possible; move clockwise; serviette in hand or on forearm, never in a pocket or on the shoulder; steady pace.

Taking the order: identify the host; stand to the right of the ordering guest; repeat the order with vintage, producer, cuvée or proprietary name, type, style or quality level; indicate which beverage is for which guest.

Glassware: tray, right hand, guest's right; same position for every guest, usually by the knife; start with the host or the guest to the host's left, then clockwise. A second bottle of the same wine: a clean tasting glass for the host to the right of the original, removed after service.

Bottle opening: two clean cuts just below the second lip; foil into your pocket; wipe the cork; remove the cork quietly with minimal movement; wipe again; cork on an underliner to the ordering guest's right.

Pouring: label facing the ordering guest, 1-1.5 oz / 30-45 ml taste; start left of the ordering guest, clockwise; a guest of honor first; the ordering guest always last; pour each guest individually without going around twice.
Non-cork closures are not presented.

Sparkling: bucket with stand to the host's right; two serviettes (one to present, dry and open; one for the lip and drips); two underliners (bottle, cork); in-air or in-the-bucket opening; cut the foil below the cage with the corkscrew blade, not the pull tab; thumb on cork and cage; never remove the cage separately; turn the bottle, not the cork; 45-degree angle if possible; ideal sound a soft hiss; handshake or bottom grip, not the punt; each glass in no more than two pours.
Decanting: three purposes: aeration, removing sediment, raising temperature by 1 to 3 degrees. The sommelier confirms with the guest, who makes the final decision.

Decanting for sediment: three serviettes (cradle, bottle lip, pouring); three underliners (cork, bottle, decanter); a bottle stored on its side goes into the cradle on its side even if the label isn't up; an upright bottle stays upright with no cradle; cut the foil without moving the bottle; pour slowly in one smooth motion, avoiding glugging; never look away; stop when fine sediment reaches the shoulder; the bottle never touches the decanter.

Double decanting: decant, rinse the bottle with a small amount of the decanted wine or a similar wine (never water), return the wine to the bottle. Splash decanting: for young full-bodied reds that seem closed; not for older or delicate wines or for sediment; inverting the bottle is acceptable.

Large formats may go into several decanters. Priming glassware or decanters (1-2 oz / 30-60 ml) only if the guest asks. Coravin: know Timeless, Pivot and Sparkling; pouring, recharging, cleaning, replacing gas canisters, changing the needle.

Beer: FIFO; repeat brewery name, beer style and brand; open at the side station; glassware: pilsner flute (pilsner), weizen glass (hefeweizen, dunkelweizen, wheat beer), goblet/snifter (Belgian strong ale, Trappist ale), tulip (IPA, barleywine, imperial stout, porter), American pint (most others), AP wine glass (many styles); tilted-glass or steady-pour technique; about 1 in. / 2-3 cm of foam; the bottle never touches the glass; ask whether the guest wants sediment from hazy beers.

Sake: modern-style service follows white wine standards; mori koboshi: ochoko inside a masu, overflow about halfway, served clockwise finishing with the ordering guest, two-handed pouring customary; nigori: invert and swirl or shake to mix the kasu; neither style is for hot sake.

Aperitifs and digestifs: served from a tray or gueridon; small tulip or copita for fortified wines, grappa, eau de vie, neat liqueurs; rocks glass for liqueurs or spirits over ice; snifter for neat oak-aged spirits (brandy, aged rum, Calvados); jigger; approach from the guest's right.

Cocktails: repeat the order with ice and garnish preferences; rim the glass first; shaken: don't overfill the shaker, no carbonated ingredients before shaking, fresh ice, no dirty rocks; stirred: mixing glass about three-quarters full of ice; built: in the serving glass in recipe order, layers from the densest ingredient over a bar spoon.

Pairing: align with the guest's preferences (red wine with shellfish if they prefer it); exam tasks: propose a beverage for a dish, evaluate strengths and weaknesses, assess suitability, explain reasoning; know classic and modern pairings, cooking techniques, iconic dishes, key ingredients and sauces of world cuisines; explain structure (acidity, tannin, body) and aromas and flavors in guest-friendly language, not technical or intimidating terms; also pair beer, sake, spirits and non-alcoholic options.
For full marks on a pairing, mention producer, vintage and full appellation, and say why the pairing works in a guest-friendly way.

Example feedback: listen to the guest for the best recommendations and sell with delicious-sounding reasoning; Practical results come by Sparkling Table, Decanting Table and Business of the Sommelier.

Expected skill set: world-class formal beverage service including still, sparkling, red wine decanting, beer, after dinner and glass pour service; global cuisine pairing salesmanship; classic cocktail production and spirits service; benchmark producers and vintages; hospitality and salesmanship.

Practical exam: Business of the Sommelier first, then Hospitality & Service immediately after; about 15-20 minutes of preparation with situations, guest notes, menus, wine list and beverage list; no writing on menus; besides cocktails, beverages poured tableside unless directed; two tables per panel; the maître d' cannot answer content questions or advise on standards; a very busy but manageable evening; suspend disbelief with signs on the prep table; face a wall if you finish your first table early; work side-on at a bar; 'Half time' and 'Two minutes' are for examiners; sequester room until the end of the day. Prepare by asking what a guest will want to know about a beverage.
Passing requires at least 60% on each section within one calendar year; a first Practical below 40% means waiting an extra year.

unverified: The 2025 standards say decanting can raise a wine's temperature '1 to 3 degrees' without naming Fahrenheit or Celsius; no unit is given here.
The Practical exam guide is dated 10.2022 and the service standards 2025; check the Court's resource library for newer versions before an exam.
The 2025 standards give no pour size for aperitifs and digestifs beyond using a jigger; none is stated here.
The Court's 2026 Upper-Level Hospitality & Service Illustrative Examples were read only to judge depth; none of their scenarios or data are used.
The forced-wait rule: the website names a third Practical below 55%; the theory guide PDF says a third Theory or Practical below 55%. Only the first-attempt 40% rule is stated here.

stops.name: Mise en place
stops.text: Clean, accurate **beverage lists**; spotless glasses polished with **linen and steam**; serviettes folded; underliners polished; tools organized. A tray that isn't non-slip gets lined with a serviette.

stops.name: The order
stops.text: Identify the **host**. Stand to the ordering guest's right. **Repeat the order** with vintage, producer, cuvée and style or quality level, and say which drink is whose.

stops.name: Glasses
stops.text: Set each glass at the guest's right, in the **same spot** for everyone, usually by the knife. Start with the host or the guest to the host's left, then go **clockwise**.

stops.name: Open and pour
stops.text: **Two cuts** below the second lip, foil in your pocket, wipe, pull quietly, wipe again, cork on an underliner. Pour a **1-1.5 oz** taste, then start left of the ordering guest and finish with them. No second lap.

read.mixup: A **second bottle** of the same wine gets a fresh tasting glass for the host. A **screwcap** isn't presented at all.

read.where: From Level 2: the Certified sparkling and decanting routine. The **2025 standards** tighten the sparkling opening and add **double decanting**, **splash decanting**, large formats and **Coravin**. The Court's example feedback scores a **Sparkling Table** and a **Decanting Table**.

stops.name: Sparkling setup
stops.text: **Two serviettes**: one to dry, present and open; one for the lip and drips. **Two underliners**: bottle and cork. Bucket on a stand to the host's right.

stops.name: Sparkling open and pour
stops.text: Cut below the cage with the **blade**, not the pull tab. Thumb on cork and cage, loosen, never let go, **turn the bottle**. Pour with a handshake or bottom grip, never the punt, in **no more than two pours** a glass.

stops.name: Decant for sediment
stops.text: The bottle stays as it was stored: upright means **no cradle**. Cut the foil without moving it, pour in **one smooth motion** without glugging, eyes on the bottle, and stop when fine sediment reaches the **shoulder**.

stops.name: Double and splash
stops.text: **Double decanting**: decant, rinse the bottle with a little of the wine (never water), pour it back. **Splash decanting**: pour hard for young, closed reds; never for old wines or sediment.

read.where: Advanced service goes beyond wine. The **2025 standards** set steps for **beer**, **sake**, **aperitifs and digestifs** and **cocktails**, and the skill set asks for classic cocktail production and spirits service. In the exam, everything but cocktails is poured **tableside** unless you're told otherwise.

stops.name: Beer
stops.text: Repeat **brewery, style and brand**. Open at the side station and choose the glass by style. Use the **tilted glass** or a **steady pour**, leaving about **1 in. / 2-3 cm** of foam. The bottle never touches the glass.

stops.name: Sake
stops.text: Modern service follows **white wine standards** in wine glasses. **Mori koboshi**: ochoko inside a masu, poured to overflow about halfway, with both hands. **Nigori**: invert and swirl to mix the **kasu**. Neither is for hot sake.

stops.name: Aperitifs and digestifs
stops.text: Serve from the guest's right. Small tulip or **copita** for fortified wine, grappa and eau de vie; **rocks glass** over ice; **snifter** for neat oak-aged spirits. Pour with a jigger.

stops.name: Cocktails
stops.text: Repeat the order with ice and garnish wishes. Rim the glass first if needed. **Built** drinks go in the serving glass in recipe order; layers start with the **densest** ingredient, poured over a bar spoon.

read.mixup: **Mori koboshi** is an overflowing pour into an ochoko set in a masu. **Nigori** is cloudy sake with kasu, mixed before pouring.

video.title: Jancis Robinson -  Food And Wine Pairing - An Understanding of Wine - BBC Maestro

keyPoints.line: The guest's taste beats the textbook pairing.
Propose, evaluate, assess, explain.
Structure and flavor, in appetizing words.
Pair beer, sake, spirits and non-alcoholic drinks too.

read.bigIdea: Delight the guest, then explain why.
read.where: Pairing is a service only the sommelier offers. The **2025 standards** put the guest's preference ahead of classic rules, and the exam tests your **reasoning** as much as your pick. The Court's example feedback says to listen to the guest, then sell with reasons that sound delicious.

stops.name: Listen first
stops.text: Start with the **guest's preferences**, the occasion and the room. A guest who wants red with shellfish gets red with shellfish.

stops.name: Know the food
stops.text: Know classic and modern pairings, **cooking techniques**, **iconic dishes**, and the key ingredients and sauces of major cuisines, so you can describe any dish with confidence.

stops.name: Explain it
stops.text: Cover **structure** (acidity, tannin, body) and how **aromas and flavors** fit together, in clear, inviting words, never intimidating ones.

stops.name: Sell it
stops.text: Name the wine with **producer, vintage and full appellation**, and offer options beyond wine: **beer, sake, spirits** and non-alcoholic drinks.

read.mixup: A **classic pairing** is a reference point. The **guest's preference** decides the pairing.
read.sayIt: The wine's bright acidity cuts the richness of the sauce and keeps each bite fresh.

Plenty of time, but every movement must count.
Everything but cocktails is poured at the table.

read.bigIdea: A busy night on the floor, two tables long.
read.where: The **Practical** is two parts on one day: **Business of the Sommelier**, then **Hospitality & Service**. The Court's example feedback reports it as a **Sparkling Table**, a **Decanting Table** and Business of the Sommelier.

stops.name: Prep
stops.text: Belongings go aside. At your review table you get about **15-20 minutes** with the situation, **guest notes**, menus, the **wine list** and the **beverage list**. Notes go on your pad, not the menus.

stops.name: The maître d'
stops.text: Walks your panel in and shows you each table. Ask where tools are or for water. Write down any **new guest notes** they give you.

stops.name: At the table
stops.text: Wait for 'Candidates, approach your tables.' Stay in your station; at a bar on the end of the side station, work **side-on** to the guests. 'Half time' and 'two minutes' are for the examiners.

stops.name: When time is called
stops.text: Your table tells you whether to keep going. Then the **sequester room** until the end of the day; no talking about the exam until you're released.

read.mixup: The **maître d'** is your guide and can't advise on standards. The **guests** are Master Sommeliers, and some play difficult roles.
